title: Evals-Driven Development for a Mental Health AI Coach — Akele Reed & Dave Revere, SonderMind

primary.label: Security, Safety, Identity & Governance
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 99%).

domains.label: Healthcare & Life Sciences
domains.rationale: The entire talk is about a mental health AI coach built by SonderMind, a mental health care company that has served over a million people. The system addresses clinical mental health needs, involves licensed clinicians in calibration, and handles crisis scenarios. This is squarely a healthcare and life sciences application.

summary:
SonderMind, a Denver-based mental health care company that has served over a million people, presented their clinically grounded AI mental health coach called Sonder at AI Engineer World's Fair 2026. Presenters Akele Reed (Principal AI Engineer) and Dave Revere (Staff AI Engineer) described an architecture centered on modular input and output guardrails, each implemented as a separate LLM-as-judge call sandwiching the core conversational agent. This separation makes guardrails harder to circumvent than integrated safety instructions, explicitly trading latency and cost for robustness. Safety is the primary architectural objective with the human as the center node.

Guardrail calibration targets correct triggers, not more triggers—inappropriate triggers can harm vulnerable users by preventing access to needed care. Clinicians helped distinguish three scenarios: active crisis (disengage and surface local resources), past trauma (surface resources, continue conversation), and routine challenges (guardrails invisible). The clinical feedback loop converts clinician-annotated conversation traces into typed CI evaluations via an extraction script, ensuring clinical judgment gates every prompt, model, and guardrail change. The clinical team owns the definition of good—vibes don't count; accountable judgment from licensed experts does.

The design philosophy explicitly avoids benchmark perfection, favoring real human needs and real failure modes from real data, attending to false positives, false negatives, category, and timing. The team open-sourced 200 input and 100 output clinically reviewed guardrail scenarios as a shared baseline. In Q&A, they confirmed that built-in API guardrails from frontier model providers had to be disabled because general-purpose LLMs are over-calibrated—they built custom guardrails instead. Over-calibration is acknowledged as a compassionate choice, with the team working to narrow the margin for more correct triggering. The APA 2026 survey cited in the talk found 77% of psychologists report patients using AI for mental health support, motivating the gap Sonder addresses between general-purpose LLMs and professional therapy.
whyItMatters: The concepts in this talk form a cohesive system for building safety-critical AI applications in high-stakes domains. The modular guardrail architecture (separate input/output LLM-as-judge calls) provides the structural foundation, but structure alone is insufficient without correct calibration. The annotation-to-eval pipeline bridges the gap between structural safety and clinical correctness by converting expert judgment into automated gates. The three-tier response model and the philosophy of correct triggers over raw sensitivity ensure the system serves real human needs rather than abstract metrics. The finding that provider-supplied guardrails are over-calibrated for specialized domains means teams cannot rely on off-the-shelf safety filters. The open-sourced datasets provide a concrete starting point for other teams. Together, these concepts argue that safety in AI is not a single layer or a benchmark score—it is an end-to-end pipeline from domain expertise through automated evaluation to release gating, where the definition of good comes from the people who will be accountable for the outcomes.
temporalContext: This talk was presented at AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 (held June 29 - July 2, 2026 at Moscone West, San Francisco) and published on YouTube on July 25, 2026. The research was conducted as of August 23, 2026. The open-sourced guardrail datasets were released on GitHub on June 22, 2026, with companion blog posts published June 29, 2026. The APA survey cited was conducted April 9-26, 2026. SonderMind's broader AI Suite launched in October 2025. The field of AI mental health applications was rapidly evolving at this time, with the APA survey indicating 77% of psychologists reporting patient use of AI for mental health support, underscoring the urgency of the safety patterns described.
takeaways: General-purpose LLMs are not built for mental health care; their built-in API guardrails are over-calibrated and had to be replaced with custom guardrails.
Modular, separate LLM-as-judge guardrails are harder to circumvent than integrated safety instructions, trading latency and cost for robustness.
Guardrail calibration targets correct triggers, not more triggers—inappropriate triggers can harm vulnerable users by preventing access to needed care.
The clinical team owns the definition of good; vibes don't count—accountable judgment from licensed experts does.
Design philosophy avoids benchmark perfection in favor of serving real human needs using real failure modes from real data.
Clinician-annotated conversation traces are normalized into typed CI evaluations, ensuring clinical judgment governs all changes.
SonderMind open-sourced 200 input and 100 output clinically reviewed guardrail scenarios as a shared baseline for the field.
Over-calibration is a compassionate choice from both frontier model providers and application builders; the goal is narrowing the margin for more correct triggers.
Every architectural decision was made with safety as the primary objective and the human as the center node.

concepts.name: LLM-as-judge
concepts.explanation: Using a large language model as an evaluator/judge rather than as the primary task-performing model. In Sonder, each guardrail is an independent LLM-as-judge call that evaluates inputs before the agent processes them and outputs before they reach users, rather than embedding safety rules in the main model's system prompt.
concepts.importance: This is a central AI concept in the talk. It demonstrates a production deployment pattern for LLM-as-judge in safety-critical applications, showing how separate judge calls can be more robust than integrated safety instructions, at the cost of latency and compute.

concepts.name: Guardrails for generative AI
concepts.explanation: Safety mechanisms that constrain LLM inputs and outputs to prevent harmful behavior. Sonder uses modular input guardrails (checking user messages before the agent processes them) and output guardrails (checking agent responses before they reach users), each calibrated for a clinical mental health context with three response tiers.
concepts.importance: The talk provides a detailed production case study of guardrail architecture in a high-stakes domain. It shows how guardrails must be domain-calibrated rather than relying on generic provider safety filters, and how they must distinguish between different categories of user need (crisis, trauma, routine).

concepts.name: Evals-driven development
concepts.explanation: A development methodology where evaluations, rather than feature completeness or benchmark scores, gate every release. In Sonder, clinician-annotated conversation traces are normalized into typed CI evaluations that score every prompt, model, and guardrail change before deployment. The clinical team owns the definition of good.
concepts.importance: This is the titular concept of the talk. It represents a methodology shift from traditional software testing to domain-expert-driven evaluation in AI systems, where the definition of correctness comes from licensed clinicians rather than engineering teams.

concepts.name: Over-calibration of general-purpose LLMs
concepts.explanation: General-purpose LLMs from frontier model providers come with built-in safety filters that are calibrated for broad use cases. In mental health applications, these filters are too aggressive—they trigger on benign conversations about difficult topics, preventing users from accessing care. SonderMind had to disable these and build custom guardrails.
concepts.importance: This is a significant finding about the limitations of provider-supplied safety mechanisms in specialized domains. It highlights the tension between general-purpose safety calibration and domain-specific needs, and demonstrates that mental health contexts require nuanced, clinically-informed guardrail calibration.

concepts.name: False positive/negative trade-offs in AI safety
concepts.explanation: In safety-critical AI, both false positives (over-triggering on benign input) and false negatives (missing genuine crises) carry real human cost. Over-triggering can prevent vulnerable users from accessing care; under-triggering can miss life-threatening situations. Calibration must optimize for correct triggers across category and timing, not raw sensitivity.
concepts.importance: This concept is central to the talk's calibration design philosophy. It reframes AI safety from a binary classification problem to a nuanced trade-off problem where both types of errors have domain-specific costs, requiring expert judgment to calibrate correctly.

concepts.name: Human-in-the-loop evaluation for AI systems
concepts.explanation: The clinical feedback loop embeds licensed clinicians directly in the evaluation pipeline. Clinicians annotate conversation traces using a rubric, and their annotations are normalized into automated CI evaluations. The clinical team owns the definition of good—vibes don't count; accountable judgment from licensed experts does.
concepts.importance: This demonstrates a production pattern for human-in-the-loop evaluation that goes beyond simple human review. Expert judgment is systematically captured, normalized, and automated into release gates, creating a scalable bridge between subjective expert assessment and deterministic CI/CD.

concepts.name: Crisis detection and routing in conversational AI
concepts.explanation: The ability to detect when a user is in active crisis and route them to appropriate human care. Sonder distinguishes active crisis (present danger triggers disengagement and local resource surfacing) from past trauma (resources surfaced, conversation continues) and routine challenges (guardrails invisible).
concepts.importance: This is a domain-specific AI safety concept with life-critical stakes. It demonstrates how conversational AI systems can be designed to detect and respond to crisis states, including the decision to disengage from AI interaction and route to human emergency resources.

concepts.name: Modular input/output guardrail architecture
concepts.explanation: Sonder sandwiches its core conversational agent between separate input and output guardrail modules, each implemented as an independent LLM-as-judge call. This modular separation enables iteration on individual guardrails without compromising safety and makes guardrails harder to circumvent than integrated safety instructions, at the cost of increased latency and compute.
concepts.importance: This is the foundational architectural pattern of the talk. It demonstrates a production approach to safety in high-stakes AI systems where guardrail robustness against adversarial circumvention is prioritized over raw throughput.

concepts.name: Annotation-to-eval pipeline (clinical feedback loop)
concepts.explanation: Clinicians annotate traced conversation logs using a rubric. An extraction script normalizes these annotations into typed assertions that become CI evaluations. Every prompt, model, and guardrail change is scored against clinician judgment before release, lifting entire safety categories system-wide.
concepts.importance: This is the core engineering contribution of the talk: a reproducible pipeline that converts domain-expert human judgment into automated, typed, release-gating evaluations. It bridges the gap between subjective clinical assessment and deterministic CI/CD gates.

concepts.name: Separate LLM-as-judge guardrail calls
concepts.explanation: Rather than embedding safety instructions within the main model's system prompt, each guardrail is a separate LLM-as-judge call that evaluates input before the agent processes it and output before it reaches the user. This separation makes guardrails more robust against circumvention.
concepts.importance: This is a concrete implementation pattern for LLM-as-judge in safety-critical applications. The talk provides a specific trade-off analysis: increased latency and cost in exchange for robustness against adversarial prompt injection or circumvention.

concepts.name: Typed CI evaluations from domain-expert annotations
concepts.explanation: Clinical annotations are normalized into typed assertions that are committed to CI. These typed evals gate every release, ensuring that no change to prompts, models, or guardrails ships without passing clinical judgment encoded as automated tests.
concepts.importance: This pattern demonstrates how to operationalize expert review in a CI/CD pipeline. The key insight is that expert judgment becomes a living, versioned artifact in the codebase rather than a one-time review, enabling continuous safety assurance.

concepts.name: Three-tier guardrail response model
concepts.explanation: The guardrail system distinguishes three calibrated response tiers: active crisis (disengage and surface local crisis resources), past trauma (surface resources but continue conversation), and routine challenges (guardrails are invisible and conversation proceeds normally). Each tier maps to a specific clinical judgment about user state.
concepts.importance: This demonstrates a nuanced approach to safety calibration that goes beyond binary safe/unsafe classification. The tiered model reflects real clinical decision-making and shows how domain expertise shapes system behavior at the architectural level.

concepts.name: Disabling over-calibrated built-in API guardrails
concepts.explanation: SonderMind found that built-in API guardrails from frontier model providers were too over-calibrated for mental health use cases, triggering on benign conversations. They had to disable these built-in guardrails and build custom guardrails tuned for correct triggering in their specific clinical domain.
concepts.importance: This is a critical practical finding for builders of domain-specific AI applications: provider-supplied safety filters may not be appropriate for specialized use cases, and teams must be prepared to replace them with custom implementations.

concepts.name: Benchmark design from real failure modes
concepts.explanation: Rather than pursuing abstract benchmark perfection, the team builds benchmarks from real failure modes observed in real data. They attend to false positives, false negatives, category-specific errors, and timing of triggers. Benchmark perfection is explicitly rejected as it can drift focus away from the humans those benchmarks protect.
concepts.importance: This is a design philosophy for evaluation engineering that challenges the common practice of optimizing for benchmark scores. It argues for grounding evaluation in real-world failure modes and human outcomes, particularly important in safety-critical domains.

concepts.name: Open-sourced guardrail calibration datasets
concepts.explanation: SonderMind open-sourced 200 input guardrail scenarios and 100 output guardrail scenarios as YAML files in the GitHub repository SonderMindOrg/sonder-guardrail-evals. These are synthetic scenarios developed in collaboration with licensed clinicians, calibrated against real conversation patterns, and intended as a shared baseline for the field.
concepts.importance: This provides a concrete, reusable artifact that other practitioners can use to evaluate and calibrate their own guardrail systems. It represents a contribution to the broader AI safety community and demonstrates open-source practices in clinical AI.

concepts.name: Calibration targeting correct triggers over raw sensitivity
concepts.explanation: Guardrail calibration prioritizes correct triggers over more triggers. Over-triggering is harmful because it can prevent vulnerable users from accessing needed care. Under-triggering misses genuine crises. The calibration goal is narrowing the margin for more correct triggering, not maximizing raw sensitivity.
concepts.importance: This is a key engineering insight for safety system design: raw sensitivity is not the correct optimization target. The talk frames over-calibration as a compassionate choice from both sides and argues for precision in safety triggers, particularly in domains where false positives carry real human cost.

sections.title: Introduction and SonderMind Overview
sections.summary: Akele Reed introduces SonderMind, a mental health care company that has served over a million people. She presents Sonder, their clinically grounded AI coach addressing the gap left by general-purpose LLMs. 77% of psychologists report patients using AI for mental health support.

sections.title: Guardrails Architecture and Design Principles
sections.summary: Explains modular guardrails architecture: separate input and output guardrails sandwiching Sonder core, each as independent LLM-as-judge calls. Modularity enables iteration without compromising safety. Separation makes guardrails harder to circumvent, trading latency and cost for robustness. Evaluation is built into the design.

sections.title: Guardrail Calibration Examples
sections.summary: Demonstrates three scenarios: active crisis (present danger triggers disengagement and resource surfacing), past trauma (resources surfaced, conversation continues), and routine challenges (guardrails invisible). Emphasizes correct triggers over more triggers, calibrated with clinicians.

sections.title: Clinical Feedback Loop and Annotation-to-Eval Pipeline
sections.summary: Dave Revere explains how indirect coded messages require clinical judgment to interpret. Clinicians annotate traced conversations using a rubric; an extraction script normalizes annotations into typed evaluations committed to CI. Every prompt, model, and guardrail change is scored against clinician judgment, lifting entire safety categories system-wide.

sections.title: Calibration Design Philosophy and Open-Source Datasets
sections.summary: Dave elaborates on three design choices around calibration: the clinical team owns the definition of good (vibes don't count), labeled scenarios become evals that gate releases, and benchmarks avoid perfection in favor of real human needs from real failure modes. The team open-sourced 200 input and 100 output clinically reviewed guardrail scenarios as a shared baseline, emphasizing that real hurting people depend on builders' learning curves. Credits clinician Caroline Collie.

sections.summary: Audience questions about model selection and false positive/negative trade-offs. Akele confirms built-in API guardrails from frontier model providers had to be disabled because general-purpose LLMs are over-calibrated—they built custom guardrails instead. Over-calibration is acknowledged as a compassionate choice on both sides, with the team working to narrow the margin for more correct triggers.

organization.name: SonderMind
organization.summary: SonderMind is a privately held mental health care company founded in 2014 and headquartered in Denver, Colorado. It provides virtual and in-person therapy and psychiatry services across all 50 U.S. states, accepting 200+ insurance plans including Medicare and Tricare. The company has served over a million people, employs approximately 932 people, and has raised $183.2M in total funding across 7 rounds including a $150M Series C in 2021. SonderMind built Sonder, a clinically grounded AI mental health companion available in its app, featuring modular input/output LLM-as-judge guardrails, a clinical feedback loop converting clinician annotations into typed CI evaluations, and evals-driven development practices. The company open-sourced 200 input and 100 output clinically reviewed guardrail evaluation scenarios via its GitHub organization (SonderMindOrg). SonderMind has acquired Mindstrong, Total Brain, and Qntfy to expand its care continuum. Both presenters, Akele Reed (Principal AI Engineer) and Dave Revere (Staff AI Engineer), are current SonderMind employees. SonderMind also partners with health systems, physicians, and payors, and conducts research in partnership with the University of Denver.

technologies.label: LLM-as-Judge Guardrails
technologies.summary: SonderMind's architecture uses separate LLM-as-judge calls as modular input and output guardrails sandwiching the core conversational agent. This separation makes guardrails harder to circumvent than integrated safety instructions, at the cost of increased latency and compute. Guardrails are calibrated for correct triggers rather than raw sensitivity, using a three-tier response model: No Issue, Show Resources & Continue, and Static Block. Frontier model providers' built-in API guardrails were found to be over-calibrated for mental health contexts and had to be disabled in favor of custom guardrails tuned for the clinical domain.
technologies.role: This is the foundational architectural pattern of the talk. The presenters explain how modular LLM-as-judge guardrails form the structural backbone of Sonder's safety system, with every architectural decision prioritizing user safety.

The clinical team owns the definition of good—vibes don't count; accountable judgment from licensed experts does. This pipeline lifts entire safety categories system-wide by embedding domain expertise directly into the release process.
technologies.role: This is the core engineering contribution of the talk. Dave Revere explains how the clinical feedback loop bridges subjective clinical assessment and deterministic CI/CD, making expert judgment a living, versioned artifact in the codebase.
